Name: Bob Wilson
Question: Is it common for elderly people to climb stairs without getting tired? What could be the reason for this?
Answer: I worked with a very fit man, he never went to the gym , but he would go hiking in the mountains, canoeing, portaging the canoes, hunting, etc. He also had a hobby farm, that he had to throw bales to the cattle etc. Every day at lunch, he would climb the stairs from the ground, to the top, 705 feet, multiple times. I don't remember exactly how many times he did it, during each lunch, I think it was 3, because he needed to save time to shower afterwards. Every year, some charity would have a stair climbing event at the Calgary tower, which isn't as high as our building. Every year he would be in the fastest ten climbers. He said it wasn't fair, because you would come up behind clumps of slow people, and have to wait to pass them. Did I mention that he was over 65. I don't know how much older, but more than just a year or two. I climbed stairs daily as well, but I was 20 years younger, and I only climbed them when I needed to. I worked on the 22nd floor, and I would climb the stairs to my office whenever I was early for work. I couldn't keep up to my friend though. If you keep doing something, it's easier to keep doing it, than to start from scratch. So if a senior can climb a lot of stairs without being tired, it's probably because they have been doing it for a while.

Question: After visiting Canada for the first time, I was rather disgusted by how mild and weak an average person there was. How would Canada manage to protect itself should the US cease to act as its shield?
Answer: Canadians are raised to be polite and well mannered. In English Canada that means not raising your voice or getting excited in a discussion. It's a very British trait, stiff upper lip, and all that, old chap. A carry over from the old days. I have many friends who weren't born in Canada, get as riled up over a friendly dominos game, as an English Canadian would in a fight. It's just how the emotions are displayed. I have friends who weren't born in Canada, ask me if they were too aggressive in their answer to a statement. Just because we act mild, doesn't mean we won't stick up for ourselves, if it comes to a fight. However you are right about the US acting as a shield. We only have 4 submarines, and only one of them has been to sea in the last 3 years, and it has less than 60 days in 3 years. Our last destroyer was decommissioned decades ago. We don't have enough people to staff both our patrol boats and our frigates, so it's only one or the other. Canada didn't have a frigate this year to send to the NATO war games. Our frigates are 28 to 37 years old, and our newest fighter jets are 36 years old.

Question: What percentage of rig workers live onboard the rig?
Answer: The vast majority of oil rigs are on land, and the workers live at home, in a camp, or a hotel. For that tiny percentage that work offshore, the majority live on board, during their rotation, which is usually between two weeks on, and two weeks off, and two months on and off. It would be very rare for anyone to live onboard for more than two months. There are some rigs close to shore, where crew boats take the crew home daily, when they finish their shifts. If someone is telling you that they live on a rig full time, they are lying.
